extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, probability, and the philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for estimating probabilities, distinguishing chance from causation, and extending empirical (derivative) laws to adjacent cases; emphasizes the primacy of causal understanding over mere frequency counts. Suitable for evaluating probabilistic reasoning in scientific and everyday inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal-possibility principle when only number of cases is known
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when we know nothing except the number of the possible and mutually excluding contingencies, and are entirely ignorant of their comparative frequency, we may have grounds, and grounds numerically appreciable, for acting on one supposition rather than on another; and this is the meaning of Probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only the count of mutually exclusive cases is known (e.g., two colors of balls and no further information), assign equal probabilities to each case; use symmetry/number-of-cases reasoning as a basis for action in the absence of further data (example: even chance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting/symmetry axiom about majority/impossibility of multiple majorities
rubrics_metrics.description: When the cases which exist are shared among several kinds, it is impossible that each of those kinds should be a majority of the whole: on the contrary, there must be a majority against each kind, except one at most; and if any kind has more than its share in proportion to the total number, the others collectively must have less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this axiom to derive relative rational probabilities from mere enumeration of mutually exclusive possibilities (example: with three colors, white vs {black, red} leads to 2:1 against white).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer improving data to complex calculation on poor data
rubrics_metrics.description: A very slight improvement in the data, by better observations, or by taking into fuller consideration the special circumstances of the case, is of more use than the most elaborate application of the calculus to probabilities founded on the data in their previous state of inferiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying sophisticated probabilistic formulas, obtain better specific knowledge about frequencies or causes; avoid misapplying the calculus of probabilities to weak/insufficient empirical bases (anti-pattern: over-reliance on formulas for witness credibility or juries without case-specific evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not generalize wide averages to individual cases without relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: The employment of [a general average] for such a purpose implies a misapprehension of the use of averages, which serve ... to protect those whose interest is at stake, against mistaking the general result of large masses of instances, but are of extremely small value as grounds of expectation in any one individual instance, unless the case be one of those in which the great majority of individual instances do not differ much from the average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a single witness or individual event, examine case-specific indicators (consistency, conduct under cross-examination, interests, partialities, capacity) rather than relying solely on population averages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware assumed independence among judges or observers
rubrics_metrics.description: The chance of a number of persons concurring in a wrong verdict is diminished the more the number is increased ... the argument forgets that ... the cause of error ... if it acted upon one judge, would be extremely likely to affect all the others in the same manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that multiplying decision-makers reduces error if judges are subject to correlated biases, shared information, or weakened responsibility; evaluate dependence and common causes of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilities as results of valid induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Such calculation of chances is grounded on an induction; and to render the calculation legitimate, the induction must be a valid one ... The fraction which mathematicians use to designate the probability of an event is the ratio of these two numbers; the ascertained proportion between the number of cases in which the event occurs and the sum of all the cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat frequency-based probabilities as inductive generalizations; ensure the induction is justified (representative sample, stable conditions) before using the frequency ratio as probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority of causal-grounded probability over mere frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability of events, as calculated from their mere frequency in past experience, affords a less secure basis for practical guidance than their probability as deduced from an equally accurate knowledge of the frequency of occurrence of their causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever possible, derive probabilities by reasoning about the causal mechanisms and the frequencies of causative factors rather than relying only on observed outcome frequencies (example: balls' draw probability supported by causal/positional considerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace’s Sixth Principle (cause-from-effect rule / Bayesian core)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an effect to be accounted for, and there being several causes which might have produced it, but of the presence of which in the particular case nothing is known; the probability that the effect was produced by any one of these causes is as the antecedent probability of the cause, multiplied by the probability that the cause, if it existed, would have produced the given effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infer causes from effects by weighting prior (antecedent) plausibility of causes by their likelihood of producing the observed effect (explicitly the antecedent × likelihood rule; illustrated in three cases). This is the operational form of Bayesian updating described in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute posterior ratios via product of antecedent and conditional probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: If causes differ in antecedent frequency and/or likelihood of producing the effect, the probability that a given cause produced the effect is proportional to the product of (antecedent probability) × (probability it would produce the effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided worked examples (Case I–III) to compute posterior probabilities as normalized products; compare causes by these products to decide which is more probable as producer of the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicative rule for repeated independent coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: If the probability of any casual coincidence, considered in itself, be 1/m, the probability that the same coincidence will be repeated n times in succession is 1/m^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate how unlikely a repeated coincidence would be under the hypothesis of mere chance by raising the single-trial probability to the nth power (examples: repeated aces with a die). Use this to judge whether observed repetition plausibly arises by chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare chance probability vs antecedent plausibility of causal explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: The probabilities ... that the fact originated in these two modes [accident or law] are as their antecedent probabilities, multiplied by the probabilities that if they existed they would produce the effect. ... The antecedent probability of the combination of mere chances ... is an appreciable quantity. The antecedent probability of the other supposition [an undiscovered law] may be unsusceptible of even an approximate valuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When weighing whether a striking coincidence is due to chance or an unknown law, compare the tiny chance of the coincidence under randomness to the (often hard-to-quantify) prior plausibility of an explanatory law; repetition can make accidental explanation implausible even if the prior for an unknown law is not numerically estimable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical criterion for inferring law from excess coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: If the number of instances in which a coincidence is observed, over and above that which would arise on the average from the mere concurrence of chances, be such that so great an amount of coincidences from accident alone would be an extremely uncommon event; we have reason to conclude that the coincidence is the effect of causation, and may be received (subject to correction from further experience) as an empirical law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the degree to which observed coincidences exceed chance-expected counts as empirical evidence for a causal law; accept provisional empirical laws when excess is sufficiently unlikely under chance, but remain open to revision with more data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative (empirical) laws are less general and certain than ultimate causal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative uniformities ... will only obtain where there exists the same collocation of those primeval causes. ... Those derivative uniformities, therefore, which are not laws of causation, are ... subject to the characteristic infirmity of empirical laws—that of being admissible only where the collocations are known by experience to be such as are requisite for the truth of the law; that is, only within the conditions of time and place confirmed by actual observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that empirical regularities often depend on specific collocations of causes and may fail when collocations change; limit claims of empirical laws to the observed conditions or closely adjacent ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of extrapolation: adjacent cases only (time and place limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: This extension of derivative laws, not causative, beyond the limits of observation can only be to adjacent cases. ... The inductions which authorize us to expect future events, grow weaker and weaker the further we look into the future, and at length become inappreciable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extend empirical laws cautiously: predictions are reliable for near-future or nearby places (adjacent cases) but become progressively weaker with temporal or spatial distance. Knowing underlying causes permits broader extrapolation than mere empirical law.
